Ants

Ant Control: What Works, What Doesn't & When to Call a Pro

By Shaw's Pest Control  ·  Wichita, KS

What's the Most Effective Way to Get Rid of Ants in Your Home?

If you're seeing ants marching across your kitchen counter or trailing along your baseboards, you're not alone. Ant infestations are among the most common pest problems Kansas homeowners face, and they can go from a minor annoyance to a major problem surprisingly fast. The challenge with ant control isn't just killing the ants you see—it's eliminating the colony you don't. Here in Wichita and across south-central Kansas, we deal primarily with three ant species that require very different approaches. Shaw's Pest Control has been helping families solve ant problems since 1987, and our Master Tech Certification means we've seen just about every scenario. This guide will help you identify which ants you're dealing with, understand why most DIY methods only make things worse, and know when it's time to call in professional help.

The Three Ant Species Kansas Homeowners Deal With Most

Understanding which ant species has invaded your home is the first step to effective ant control. Each species has different nesting habits, food preferences, and vulnerabilities.

Odorous house ants are the most common culprits. These small brown or black ants earn their name from the rotten coconut smell they release when crushed. They're attracted to sweet foods and moisture, often entering through tiny cracks near plumbing or windows. Their colonies can contain thousands of workers and multiple queens, which is why killing the ants you see rarely solves the problem.

Carpenter ants are larger—up to half an inch long—and typically black or red-and-black. Unlike termites, they don't eat wood, but they do excavate it to build their nests. If you see large black ants in your home, especially near water-damaged wood or in the evening hours when they're most active, you may have a structural problem developing. Carpenter ant damage happens slowly but can compromise wood framing, window sills, and roof structures over time.

Pavement ants are the small brown ants you'll often see near driveways, sidewalks, and foundation cracks. They nest in or under concrete slabs and enter homes through foundation gaps. While they're less destructive than carpenter ants, pavement ant colonies are persistent and can quickly establish satellite nests inside your walls if conditions are right.

Why Store-Bought Ant Sprays Usually Make Things Worse

Most homeowners try DIY ant control first, and that makes sense. You see ants, you spray them, problem solved—except it's not. Here's what actually happens.

When you spray visible ants with a retail insecticide, you kill the foragers. But those foragers represent maybe 10% of the colony. The queen, the eggs, the larvae, and thousands of other workers remain safely tucked away in the nest—often inside your walls, under your foundation, or outside near your home's perimeter. The colony doesn't just survive; it adapts.

Many ant species, particularly odorous house ants, respond to threats by "budding." When the colony detects danger (chemical sprays definitely qualify), it splits into multiple colonies. A single queen and a group of workers break off and establish a new nest elsewhere in your home. What started as one colony becomes three or four, and your ant problem multiplies.

The professionals at Shaw's Pest Control use a completely different approach. Instead of repellent sprays that scatter colonies, we use non-repellent treatments that ants can't detect. Foragers walk through the treatment, carry it back to the nest, and transfer it to other ants through contact and feeding. This process eliminates the entire colony, including the queen. We also use targeted baiting strategies where appropriate—not the gel baits you buy at the hardware store, but professional-grade baits with active ingredients and attractants that aren't available to consumers.

When DIY Works and When You Need Professional Ant Control

There's a narrow window where do-it-yourself methods can work, and it's important to recognize it.

If you've spotted fewer than a dozen ants over several days, they're not trailing (just randomly wandering), and you can identify and seal their entry point, you might have caught the problem before a colony established itself. Clean the area thoroughly with vinegar to disrupt pheromone trails, seal any cracks with caulk, and monitor for a week. If no new ants appear, you may have dodged the bullet.

However, if you're seeing ant trails—those organized lines of ants following the same path—you have an established colony with active foraging routes. That means there are potentially thousands of ants you're not seeing. If ants keep coming back after you clean or spray, if you're seeing them in multiple rooms, or if you're finding ants near water sources like sinks, dishwashers, or bathrooms, you're past the DIY stage.

Carpenter ants always warrant professional attention. By the time you see carpenter ants inside your home regularly, they've likely been nesting in your structure long enough to cause damage. Our ant control services in Wichita include thorough inspections to locate nests, assess any wood damage, and develop a treatment plan that addresses both the immediate infestation and the conditions that attracted them.

Ant Control in Wichita: What Local Homeowners Should Know

Ant activity in the Wichita area follows predictable seasonal patterns, and understanding these patterns helps with both prevention and treatment timing.

Spring is when most ant problems become visible. As temperatures warm and colonies become active after winter, foragers search for food and water to support the colony's rapid growth. This is when you'll notice those first scouts in your kitchen. Early spring is actually the best time for professional ant control in Wichita—treating colonies before they reach peak size in summer is more effective and prevents the breeding season from expanding the problem.

Summer heat drives ants indoors searching for water and cooler conditions, which is why kitchens and bathrooms become hotspots. Fall brings a second surge as ants stockpile food before winter, and some species actually move their colonies indoors to overwinter in wall voids or insulation.

Our ant control services in Andover and throughout the service area account for these patterns. We don't just treat the ants you're seeing today—we implement strategies that address the colony life cycle and prevent re-infestation. With three State Certifications and Master Tech Certification, we use methods and products that are both effective and safe for your family and pets.

Frequently Asked Questions

What attracts ants to my house?

Ants are primarily attracted by food, water, and shelter. Even tiny crumbs, sticky spills, or pet food left out can draw scout ants. Moisture problems like leaky pipes, poor drainage, or high humidity create ideal conditions. Once ants find a reliable resource, they lay pheromone trails that recruit hundreds more workers to the same location.

How long does professional ant control take to work?

Most homeowners notice significant reduction in ant activity within 3-5 days of professional treatment. Complete colony elimination typically takes 2-3 weeks, depending on species and colony size. Non-repellent treatments work slowly but thoroughly—foragers need time to spread the treatment throughout the colony and reach the queen.

Can ants damage my home like termites do?

Carpenter ants can cause structural damage, though they work more slowly than termites. They excavate wood to create nesting galleries, weakening structural members over time. Unlike termites, carpenter ants prefer wood that's already water-damaged or decaying. Other ant species don't damage structures, but their nesting habits can compromise insulation effectiveness.

Why do I still see ants after treatment?

Seeing ants for several days after treatment is normal and actually indicates the treatment is working. Non-repellent products allow ants to continue their normal activity while unknowingly spreading the treatment through the colony. If you're still seeing active trails two weeks after treatment, that indicates either a very large colony or a secondary colony that needs additional treatment.

What's the difference between ant baits and sprays?

Ant baits use attractive food matrices mixed with slow-acting insecticides. Foragers carry bait back to share with the colony, including the queen. Baits eliminate entire colonies but take time. Sprays kill on contact but only affect ants directly contacted—they don't reach the colony. Repellent sprays can make problems worse by causing colonies to split.

How can I prevent ants from coming back?

Prevention combines sanitation and exclusion. Store food in sealed containers, clean up spills immediately, and don't leave pet food out overnight. Fix plumbing leaks and drainage problems that create moisture. Seal cracks in your foundation, around utility penetrations, and where sidewalks meet your house. Keep tree branches and shrubs trimmed away from your home's exterior.
